title: Duals of complexes with finite locally constant cohomology
statement:
Let $\lambda=\mathbf F_\ell$, let $T$ be a scheme on which
$\ell$ is invertible, and let $C$ be an ordinary
bounded derived complex
of etale $\lambda$-sheaves. Suppose all $\mathcal H^q(C)$
are finite locally constant. Its
derived internal dual
$C^\vee=R\mathcal Hom_\lambda(C,\lambda_T)$ has finite locally
constant cohomology, with

$$
\mathcal H^q(C^\vee)
=\mathcal Hom_\lambda(\mathcal H^{-q}(C),\lambda_T).
$$

For every scheme morphism $v:T'\to T$, the canonical morphism
$v^*C^\vee\to (v^*C)^\vee$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text: Work on a small equivalent site in the module universe, using [def-weil-size-convention]. Use the K-injective definition of derived internal Hom, rather than the pro-etale operations definition. Restriction to a slice site commutes with this construction: choose a K-injective resolution $I$ of the second argument. Its restriction $I|_U$ is K-injective by [lem-pur-kinjective-restrict-localized]. The restriction of the Hom complex is the Hom complex of the restrictions: evaluated on $V/U$, each sheaf Hom consists of maps on the same further slice site, and products and the differential are computed sectionwise. The differential is $d_I f-(-1)^n f d_P$ on both sides. This proves the restriction identification, including its naturality, from [def-pur-sheaf-hom] and [def-pur-hom-complex]. Restriction preserves kernels sectionwise and preserves cokernels because local lifts and relations are checked on precisely the same covering families in each slice. Thus the restricted resolution is still a quasi-isomorphism.

Let $E$ be a finite locally constant $\lambda $-module sheaf. By the lisse definition it is locally the constant sheaf of a finite-dimensional $\lambda $-vector space. Choosing a basis identifies it on a trivializing etale covering with $\lambda ^r$, for finite $r$ which can vary with the covering member. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-site-bounded-free-rhom-model] with $P=\lambda ^r[0]$ and $N=\lambda [0]$. Its Hom complex is $\lambda ^r$ in degree zero and zero elsewhere. Step 1 identifies this with the restriction of $R\mathcal Hom(E,\lambda _T)$. Thus this derived Hom has no cohomology outside degree zero, and degree zero is the ordinary sheaf Hom $\mathcal  Hom(E,\lambda _T)$, by its definition. This sheaf is locally $\lambda ^r$, hence finite locally constant. This includes $r=0$. No global Ext group is asserted to vanish.

Write $D(K)=R\mathcal Hom(K,\lambda _T)$. Choose $a\leq  b$ with $\mathcal  H^i(C)=0$ outside $[a,b]$, and induct on the interval length, with the zero object as base case. The standard truncation triangle is $A\to  C\to  B\to  A[1]$, where $A=\tau_{\leq  b-1}C$ and $B=\mathcal  H^b(C)[-b]$. The kernel description of canonical truncation gives $\mathcal  H^i(A)=\mathcal  H^i(C)$ for $i<b$, zero for $i\geq  b$, and the displayed identification of $B$. Explicitly, replace $C$ by $P=\tau_{\leq b}C$, whose inclusion is a quasi-isomorphism. The quotient $P/\tau_{\leq b-1}P$ has only the terms $\operatorname{im}(d^{b-1})$ in degree $b-1$ and $\ker(d^b)$ in degree $b$, with the inclusion differential. Its projection onto $\mathcal H^b(C)[-b]$ is a quasi-isomorphism: the kernel is the two-term identity complex on $\operatorname{im}(d^{b-1})$. This gives the stated top truncation canonically in the derived category. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-ringed-internal-hom-exact-restriction] to get $D(B)\to  D(C)\to  D(A)\to  D(B)[1]$. For a sheaf $E$, the degree-$n$ terms of the Hom complexes for $D(E[-b])$ and $D(E)[b]$ are both $\mathcal Hom(E,I^{n+b})$. Their differentials are respectively $d_I$ and $(-1)^b d_I$; multiplication in degree $n$ by $(-1)^{bn}$ is a chain isomorphism. Thus $D(E[-b])=D(E)[b]$. Step 2 places $D(B)$ only in degree $-b$, while induction places $D(A)$ in $[-b+1,-a]$. In the cohomology long exact sequence, $\mathcal  H^{-b-1}(D(A))$ and $\mathcal  H^{-b}(D(A))$ vanish, so $\mathcal  H^{-b}(D(B))\to \mathcal  H^{-b}(D(C))$ is an isomorphism. For $q\geq -b+1$ the two surrounding terms from $D(B)$ vanish, so $\mathcal  H^q(D(C))\to \mathcal  H^q(D(A))$ is an isomorphism; below $-b$ all terms vanish. This proves the formula in the statement and the bound $[-b,-a]$, using the canonical edge identifications of the truncations. The zero case is represented by the zero complex. Step 2 proves finite local constancy of all the resulting cohomology sheaves.

proof.text: For $v:T'\to  T$, [prop-weil-pbc-inverse-image-modules-exact] identifies $v^*$ with exact module inverse image and identifies $v^{-1}\lambda _T$ with $\lambda _{T'}$. Consequently pullback commutes with kernels, images and cokernels. Termwise pullback therefore commutes with cohomology and canonical truncation, and carries quasi-isomorphisms and cone triangles to quasi-isomorphisms and cone triangles. It preserves the cohomological bounds. Pulling back an etale trivializing covering gives a covering of $T'$ on which the pulled-back sheaf has the same finite constant module values.

proof.text: Describe the canonical comparison explicitly. Represent $K$ by $P$, resolve $\lambda _T$ by a K-injective complex $I$, and choose a K-injective resolution $v^*I\to  J$. Exactness of pullback means that $J$ represents $\lambda _{T'}$. To construct the sheaf-Hom comparison, an inverse-image presheaf generator represented by a section $f$ of $\mathcal Hom(F,G)$ on an etale neighborhood $U$ is sent to the pulled-back map $v^*F|_{U\times_T T'}\to v^*G|_{U\times_T T'}$. Restricting $f$ and then pulling back gives the restriction of this map; addition and scalar multiplication also commute. These maps respect the presheaf relations and glue after sheafification, by [def-weil-pbc-inverse-image] and [def-pur-sheaf-hom]. Applied degreewise, this gives $v^*\mathcal  Hom(P^i,I^j)\to \mathcal  Hom(v^*P^i,v^*I^j)$. Using the projections from the product defining each Hom-complex term, then postcomposing with $v^*I\to  J$, gives the chain map $v^*\mathcal  Hom^\bullet(P,I)\to \mathcal  Hom^\bullet(v^*P,J)$ representing the comparison. Its differential commutes because pullback preserves addition and composition and the differential is $d_I f-(-1)^n f d_P$. The map is pullback of evaluation, hence is the canonical comparison. On a neighborhood trivializing $E$ as $\lambda ^r$, steps 1-2 identify this comparison with the identity on the $r$ coordinate functionals. The base-changed covering covers $T'$, so each cohomology sheaf map is an isomorphism at every geometric stalk. Apply [lemma-weil-pbc-geometric-stalk-conservative] to the underlying abelian sheaves. The comparison for $E$ is therefore a quasi-isomorphism and so an isomorphism in the derived category. The degreewise sign $(-1)^{bn}$ from step 3 commutes with pullback and postcomposition, so the comparison for $E[-b]$ is the shift by $b$ of that for $E$, and is an isomorphism.

Induct again through the triangle $A\to  C\to  B\to  A[1]$ of step 3. Pulling back its dual triangle gives $v^*D(B)\to  v^*D(C)\to  v^*D(A)\to  v^*D(B)[1]$. Dualizing the pulled-back triangle gives $D'(v^*B)\to  D'(v^*C)\to  D'(v^*A)\to  D'(v^*B)[1]$, where $D'=R\mathcal Hom(-,\lambda _{T'})$. The step-5 comparisons form a morphism of these triangles: for a chain map $f:P\to Q$, the cone has terms $Q^n\oplus P^{n+1}$ and differential matrix $\begin{pmatrix}d_Q&f\0&-d_P\end{pmatrix}$. In the Hom differential $d_I h-(-1)^n h d_{\mathrm{Cone}(f)}$, applying pullback and postcomposition with the fixed chain map $v^*I\to J$ preserves each of these four entries, including the minus sign. The cone inclusions and projections are coordinate inclusions and projections and hence commute as well. Thus the square for the connecting arrow commutes with the same shift sign as the other squares. The endpoint comparisons are isomorphisms by induction and step 5. More explicitly, the cohomology sequences and the bounds of step 3 identify degree $-b$ with the $B$ terms and degrees at least $-b+1$ with the $A$ terms, compatibly with this morphism of triangles. Below $-b$ both sides vanish. Every cohomology map of the middle comparison is an isomorphism, so that comparison is an isomorphism in the derived category. This proves the assertion for arbitrary $v$.
